The next sentence, on escaping the eternal fire, fits either reading.

Lake's own Loeb edition of Eusebius (1926) prints tou Christou sou, 'your Christ', at 4.15.33, so Eusebius's copies themselves differ here; the NPNF English has 'in the cup of Christ'.

a: with him and the Holy Spirit
t: 'With him and the Holy Spirit' or 'with him, in the Holy Spirit'?
p: Eusebius's copy gives glory 'in the Holy Spirit', not 'with ... the Holy Spirit'.

why: Lake prints the manuscripts without a footnote. Both name Father, Son and Spirit; the manuscripts set the Spirit beside the Son, Eusebius's copy names the Spirit as the one in whom glory is given (see the note at 14:3). The NPNF English: 'through whom, with him, in the Holy Spirit, be glory unto you'.

a: like a loaf in the oven, or like gold and silver
p: Eusebius's copy has no loaf: only gold and silver refined in a furnace.

readings.w: Lake's text (the Greek manuscripts; his footnotes note no difference here)

readings.orig: ἀλλ’ ὡς χρυσὸς καὶ ἄργυρος ἐν καμίνῳ πυρούμενος
readings.en: but like gold and silver being refined in a furnace

why: Lake prints the manuscripts without a footnote. The loaf is the image Claude's theory on the chapter page builds on, and it stands in the manuscripts only; whether Eusebius's copy lacked it or Eusebius left it out, the texts opened here do not say.

a: a dove came out, and so much blood
p: The manuscripts have a dove come out with the blood. Eusebius has only blood; one scholar emended the dove away.

readings.w: The Greek manuscripts as Lake prints them (his footnote names only Eusebius as lacking the words)
readings.en: there came out a dove and a quantity of blood
readings.plain: a dove came out, and so much blood

readings.w: Eusebius, Church History 4.15.39 (E), Greek of Lake's Loeb edition (1926)

readings.w: Conjecture of Wordsworth (in no manuscript), reported in Lake's footnote
readings.en: there came out around the sword-hilt a quantity of blood
readings.plain: so much blood came out around the hilt

why: Lake prints the dove, the reading of the manuscripts. Eusebius quotes the letter at length but has no dove (and has 'sword' for 'dagger', see the next entry), which may mean his copy lacked it, or that he left it out. Wordsworth's guess, that peristera kai ('a dove and') is a miscopying of peri styraka ('around the hilt'), would explain the dove as a scribal slip, but no witness has it. The Plain English Translation follows the manuscripts, as Lake does.
b: Lake explains the dove as the belief 'that the spirit appears at death in the form of a bird' (see the note). Readers who doubt the miracles of the account often point to this verse first.

p: The manuscripts say 'dagger'; Eusebius's copy says 'sword'.

readings.w: Lake's text (the Greek manuscripts; his footnotes note no difference here)

p: Eusebius and two manuscripts read 'catholic'; the Moscow manuscript and the Latin read 'holy'.

readings.w: Eusebius (E) and Codices Baroccianus and Hierosolymitanus (b s), Lake's text
readings.orig: ἐπίσκοπος τῆς ἐν Σμύρνῃ καθολικῆς ἐκκλησίας
readings.en: overseer of the catholic church in Smyrna

readings.w: Codex Mosquensis (m) and the Latin (L; Lake's footnote puts the L in parentheses)
readings.orig: ἐπίσκοπος τῆς ἐν Σμύρνῃ ἁγίας ἐκκλησίας
readings.en: overseer of the holy church in Smyrna

why: Lake prints 'catholic' with Eusebius and two manuscripts; his footnote does not say what p and v read. Eusebius's Greek has 'catholic' (4.15.39, Lake's Loeb text) and, a few words earlier, lacks 'martyr Polycarp' ('the most marvelous teacher'). 'Catholic church in Smyrna' is the harder phrase: elsewhere in the letter 'catholic' means worldwide (1:0; 8:1; 19:2), and a scribe may have changed it to the commoner 'holy'. If 'catholic' is right, it means the true church, the one in communion with the whole, as it exists in Smyrna. Lake's footnote: 'If the reading "Catholic" be right, this and the instance on p. 322 [8:1] are the earliest clear examples of this use of the word (but cf. Ignatius, Smyrn. viii.).'

p: Eusebius spells the name 'Dalce'.

p: In the manuscripts the evil one prompted Nicetes; in Eusebius's copy 'certain people' did.

why: Lake prints the manuscripts without a footnote. In them the subject runs on from 17:1, the evil one; Eusebius's copy names human prompters, and the letter then says 'they said this at the prompting and urging of the Jews' in both. Eusebius also has hēgemoni, 'governor', for the manuscripts' archonti, 'ruler', which the Plain English Translation already renders 'governor'. The NPNF English: 'certain ones secretly suggested to Nicetes'.

p: With 'to whom', the doxology is addressed to Jesus Christ; without it, to God.

p: In place of 22:2-3, the Moscow manuscript has a longer note about Irenaeus, Marcion and a voice heard in Rome. The two verses go together.

readings.w: Codices Baroccianus, Parisinus and Hierosolymitanus (b p s), Lake's text
readings.orig: Ταῦτα μετεγράψατο μὲν Γάϊος ἐκ τῶν Εἰρηναίου, μαθητοῦ τοῦ Πολυκάρπου, ὃς καὶ συνεπολιτεύσατο τῷ Εἰρηναίῳ. ἐγὼ δὲ Σωκράτης ἐν Κορίνθῳ ἐκ τῶν Γαΐου ἀντιγράφων ἔγραψα. ἡ χάρις μετὰ πάντων.

readings.plain: Gaius copied these things from the papers of Irenaeus, a disciple of Polycarp, and Gaius had also lived with Irenaeus. And I, Socrates, wrote them out in Corinth from the copies of Gaius. Grace be with all.

readings.w: Codex Mosquensis (m), the ending Lake prints after the text ('Epilogus alius e codice Mosquensi descriptus', sections 2-6)
readings.orig: Ταῦτα μετεγράψατο μὲν Γάϊος ἐκ τῶν Εἰρηναίου συγγραμμάτων, ὃς καὶ συνεπολιτεύσατο τῷ Εἰρηναίῳ, μαθητῇ γεγονότι τοῦ ἁγίου Πολυκάρπου. οὗτος γὰρ ὁ Εἰρηναῖος, κατὰ τὸν καιρὸν τοῦ μαρτυρίου τοῦ ἐπισκόπου Πολυκάρπου γενόμενος ἐν Ῥώμῃ, πολλοὺς ἐδίδαξεν· οὗ καὶ πολλὰ συγγράμματα κάλλιστα καὶ ὀρθότατα φέρεται, ἐν οἷς μέμνηται Πολυκάρπου, ὅτι παρ᾽ αὐτοῦ ἔμαθεν, ἱκανῶς τε πᾶσαν αἵρεσιν ἤλεγξεν καὶ τὸν ἐκκλησιαστικὸν κανόνα καὶ καθολικόν, ὡς παρέλαβεν παρὰ τοῦ ἁγίου, καὶ παρέδωκεν. λέγει δὲ καὶ τοῦτο· ὅτι συναντήσαντός ποτε τῷ ἁγίῳ Πολυκάρπῳ Μαρκίωνος, ἀφ᾽ οὗ οἱ λεγόμενοι Μαρκιωνισταί, καὶ εἰπόντος· Ἐπιγίνωσκε ἡμᾶς, Πολύκαρπε, εἶπεν αὐτὸς τῷ Μαρκίωνι· Ἐπιγινώσκω, ἐπιγινώσκω τὸν πρωτότοκον τοῦ σατανᾶ. καὶ τοῦτο δὲ φέρεται ἐν τοῖς τοῦ Εἰρηναίου συγγράμμασιν, ὅτι ᾗ ἡμέρᾳ καὶ ὥρᾳ ἐν Σμύρνῃ ἐμαρτύρησεν ὁ Πολύκαρπος, ἤκουσεν φωνὴν ἐν τῇ Ῥωμαίων πόλει ὑπάρχων ὁ Εἰρηναῖος ὡς σάλπιγγος λεγούσης· Πολύκαρπος ἐμαρτύρησεν. Ἐκ τούτων οὖν, ὡς προλέλεκται, τῶν τοῦ Εἰρηναίου συγγραμμάτων Γάϊος μετεγράψατο, ἐκ δὲ τῶν Γαΐου ἀντιγράφων Ἰσοκράτης ἐν Κορίνθῳ. ἐγὼ δὲ πάλιν Πιόνιος ἐκ τῶν Ἰσοκράτους ἀντιγράφων ἔγραψα κατὰ ἀποκάλυψιν τοῦ ἁγίου Πολυκάρπου ζητήσας αὐτά, συναγαγὼν αὐτὰ ἤδη σχεδὸν ἐκ τοῦ χρόνου κεκμηκότα, ἵνα κἀμὲ συναγάγῃ ὁ κύριος Ἰησοῦς Χριστὸς μετὰ τῶν ἐκλεκτῶν αὐτοῦ εἰς τὴν ἐπουράνιον αὐτοῦ βασιλείαν· ᾧ ἡ δόξα σὺν τῷ πατρὶ καὶ τῷ υἱῷ καὶ τῷ ἁγίῳ πνεύματι εἰς τοὺς αἰῶνας τῶν αἰώνων. ἀμήν.
readings.en: Gaius copied from the writings of Irenaeus, who was in Rome at the time; Irenaeus's story of Marcion; the trumpet voice in Rome; Isocrates copied in Corinth; Pionius copied from Isocrates
readings.plain: Gaius copied these things from the writings of Irenaeus. He had also lived with Irenaeus, who had been a disciple of the holy Polycarp. For this Irenaeus, at the time of the martyrdom of the overseer Polycarp, was in Rome and taught many. Many very fine and very correct writings of his are in circulation, in which he mentions Polycarp, saying that he learned from him. He thoroughly refuted every heresy, and he handed on the church's catholic rule as he had received it from the saint. He also says this: Marcion, from whom the so-called Marcionites come, once met the holy Polycarp and said, 'Recognize us, Polycarp.' He said to Marcion, 'I recognize you, I recognize the firstborn of Satan.' This too is told in the writings of Irenaeus: on the day and at the hour when Polycarp was martyred in Smyrna, Irenaeus, who was in the city of the Romans, heard a voice like a trumpet saying, 'Polycarp has been martyred.' From these writings of Irenaeus, then, as was said before, Gaius made a copy, and from the copies of Gaius, Isocrates in Corinth. And I, Pionius, wrote again from the copies of Isocrates, after searching for them in keeping with a revelation from the holy Polycarp. I gathered them together when they were nearly worn out with age, so that the Lord Jesus Christ may also gather me with his chosen ones into his heavenly kingdom. To him be glory with the Father and the Son and the Holy Spirit forever and ever. Amen.

why: Lake prints the ending of b p s as the text and gives m's ending separately ('Instead of the two paragraphs ταῦτα μετεγράψατο—ἀμήν m has the alternative conclusion given below'). The Moscow ending is longer and fuller: it adds that Irenaeus was in Rome when Polycarp died, repeats his story of Marcion (found in Against Heresies 3.3.4), tells of a voice like a trumpet that Irenaeus heard in Rome, and names the Corinthian copyist Isocrates instead of Socrates. None of the texts opened for this page (Irenaeus, Against Heresies 3.3.4; Eusebius, Church History 5.20) has the trumpet story. In b p s the English 'papers' is supplied: the Greek says only 'from those of Irenaeus' (ek tōn Eirēnaiou); the Moscow ending says 'from the writings of Irenaeus' (syngrammatōn).
b: The Moscow manuscript, which often has the better text elsewhere (Lake), is here the only witness to its ending, so the two endings cannot be weighed by manuscript support. Both are later notes, not part of Smyrna's letter (Lake at 20:2).

a: And I, Pionius, wrote them out again from the copy just named, after searching for them, because blessed Polycarp showed them to me in a revelation, as I will explain in what follows. I gathered them together when they were nearly worn out with age, so that the Lord Jesus Christ may also gather me with his chosen ones into his heavenly kingdom. To him be glory with the Father and the Holy Spirit forever and ever. Amen.
t: Pionius's note, missing in the Moscow manuscript
p: The Moscow manuscript has its own ending instead of 22:2-3 (see 22:2). The two verses go together.

readings.w: Codices Baroccianus, Parisinus and Hierosolymitanus (b p s), Lake's text
